co_talus_field.blurb: A slope of boulders just under a small summit in the Bigfoots, a remote pocket of Pike National Forest reached off Rampart Range Road and sitting around 9,500 feet. The stone is clean granite with sharp, cleaved features, and the place is all bouldering, with roughly eighteen problems. Most fall between V1 and V5, with a couple of harder tests at the top end, so it suits a mixed group that wants a quiet day away from the usual crowds. Expect no maintained trails and some navigating on talus and through burned timber, so it rewards a patient, self-reliant visit rather than a quick session.

co_vulture_walls.blurb: One of the taller faces in Castlewood Canyon State Park south of Denver, set between the dam and the falls area where the canyon narrows toward its point. The routes are mostly traditional lines, with a handful of bolted sport climbs and a lone top-rope. Difficulty runs from easy 5.6 up to 5.12, but the bulk of the climbing clusters in the 5.10 and 5.11 range, so it fits climbers who have outgrown the park's shorter beginner walls. The creek-bottom trail gives the quickest way in, crossing the stream above the falls and angling uphill to the south.

co_der_freischutz.blurb: A compact, scenic formation on the shoulder of Dinosaur Mountain above Bear Canyon in the Boulder Flatirons, around 6,700 feet. Routes are short, topping out near fifty feet, and the mix covers trad, sport and a couple of top-ropes. The grades stretch from an easy scramble-grade ridge to hard 5.13, though most lines are mid-range or tougher, with a cluster in the 5.11s. The southwest face catches the afternoon sun and has anchors for a quick rappel off the west side. Reaching it means a faint path up a wooded gully from the main trail, ending at a flat boulder below the face.
